sm: The CrossPolitic hosts open a midterm autopsy show with guest Steve Deace. Deace says President Trump broke covenant with his base and paid a price, as other presidents did before. He cites George H. W. Bush's broken no-new-taxes pledge, Bill Clinton's tax hikes and Hillary care before the 1994 wipeout, and George W. Bush's troubles before 2006 and 2008. He says that if Trump reinvents himself the way Clinton did, Republicans will win in 2028 no matter whom they nominate, and that Trump's approval needs to reach the mid-forties. Otherwise he predicts a heavy loss.

Deace warns Democrats could win with someone like Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez if Trump does not repair the broken covenant, saying nobody was held accountable and everything costs more, partly because of a Middle East war. He says the Republican Party cannot govern nationally because corporate interests and the base want different things, and calls it a big tarp rather than a big tent. He blames primary voters, weak establishment endorsements, and Trump's style as a disruptor rather than a manager. Host Gabe says Republicans with majorities repeatedly deliver little, while Deace says many Republicans simply do not agree with the base.

The hosts say many Republican senators do not hold the base's convictions, and that even evangelical lawmakers often do not know what the Bible says about government, as seen in Idaho Family Policy Center work. Deace says the loss was national, citing ballot measures in states like Washington and Colorado, a state sending its first Democratic senator to Washington since 1932, and tougher SAVE Act measures passing. He calls it a Watergate-level rejection and says Trump broke promises on affordability, draining the swamp and foreign wars. All agree Texas was partly its own case, with Governor Abbott's unkept property tax promises hurting Republicans there.

Deace says Texas showed a generational failure of a technocratic party, noting a fifth of early voters had skipped recent primaries. He argues James Talarico drew young voters who want a redefined Christianity, calling it wicked soul craft over no soul craft, and says Republicans must return to old-time religion. The hosts contrast DeSantis, who governed boldly and grew his base, with Abbott, whose vote stayed flat. Deace says primaries are easier once incumbents leave, but that Republicans cannot let the party fail because Democrats would turn states into California. He adds that young men lack a path to home ownership, with a median first-time buyer age of forty-two.

Deace says choosing between parties is like Russian roulette, but that DeSantis proved politics can move culture on the right by governing with conviction, even moving Palm Beach County. Co-host Knox asks what a reinvented Trump would do. Deace says he would replace chief of staff Susie Wiles with Stephen Miller, secure a credible voter fraud conviction, using the Alaska case, and fire Howard Lutnick, then prosecute someone from the Epstein list as acts of atonement. He says Democrats will offer only Medicare for all and taxes, so Republicans can reclaim affordability. Knox asks how to restore belief in free markets.

Deace proposes asking Generation X to be the we'll-take-it generation, accepting that they will not get Social Security and moving those born after 1980 into Trump accounts so their children are free. Asked about Iran, he says he detests the regime but thinks Trump hoped for regime change on the cheap without a plan for what comes next, citing Kurds, the Revolutionary Guard and the shah's grandson. He says the blockade raised fuel prices and cost the election. He warns that cutting and running would be a propaganda win for Iran, and urges a show of force and a way out framed as a win.

Deace finishes, and the hosts thank him. Knox and Gabe reflect that Trump broke covenant, tying it to Old Testament covenant imagery and the violence of broken covenants such as divorce. They say the autopsy is really of the people, whose leaders reflect them, pointing to churches abandoning biblical teaching. They link the Nvidia chief executive's adultery to national risk. Knox says conservatives now want their own fascism rather than free markets, and that they will not beat China with better socialism. They argue young people no longer believe opportunity exists.

The hosts say the only way to beat China is with free markets and free people, and that a nation of covenant breakers should not expect a covenant-keeping president. They link sexual sin and economic sin, quoting First Thessalonians chapter four, and note divorce, adultery and pornography rates. Knox says the first crime scene in the Nvidia affair was the family, and the nation the second victim. Gabe says Republicans cannot have honest conversations about conservatism, citing Idaho's governor Brad Little, Congressman Russ Fulcher and Ken Paxton's affairs. They say virtue must begin in homes.

Gabe says he wants to go back to Bible 101 with politicians, and that politics now is calculation rather than doing the right thing, as DeSantis did. Knox says virtue must be argued through culture, with well-trained children honoring their parents, working with their families and producing value. He says families are the engine of the economy, and that business can win favor without needing votes. Both say they focus on what they control, such as their kids, marriages and work, and that culture changes as people faithfully take dominion under Christ.

Knox says God gives parents children to teach Deuteronomy six and to give back to God better than they found them, and that the home is the primary way saints are grown. He says Jensen Huang was never elected, yet his unfaithfulness threatens everyone, and that men are qualified for leadership by how they manage their families. He argues a lack of Christian wealth comes from not facing the challenge of homeschooling on one income and trusting God to provide. He says faithful men refuse bribes and protect society. The hosts close by urging listeners to marry, have children, baptize them and love God and neighbor.
